Dedekind's construction

Definitions

For now, we assume that the rational numbers Q\mathbb{Q}Q already exist, together with their arithmetic and usual order <Q<_{\mathbb{Q}}<Q​. Our aim is to construct the real numbers from them.

We mark rational addition, subtraction, and multiplication by +Q+_{\mathbb{Q}}+Q​, −Q-_{\mathbb{Q}}−Q​, and ⋅Q\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}⋅Q​. Fractions and squares of rational numbers retain their usual notation. Operations on the real numbers we construct will carry no such subscript.

The intuition behind a Dedekind cut is to locate a number by specifying all the rational numbers lying strictly to its left. Such a description can locate a rational point, but it can also locate a gap in Q\mathbb{Q}Q. The boundary need not itself be rational. We retain only the left-hand set, since its complement determines the right-hand side.

Definition 1 — Dedekind left sets

A Dedekind left set is a subset r^⊆Q\hat{r}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}r^⊆Q satisfying the following conditions.

  1. Nonempty and proper. ∅≠r^≠Q\varnothing\ne\hat{r}\ne\mathbb{Q}∅=r^=Q.
  2. Downward closed. If p∈r^p\in\hat{r}p∈r^ and q∈Qq\in\mathbb{Q}q∈Q satisfy q<Qpq<_{\mathbb{Q}}pq<Q​p, then q∈r^q\in\hat{r}q∈r^.
  3. No greatest element. For every p∈r^p\in\hat{r}p∈r^, there exists q∈r^q\in\hat{r}q∈r^ such that p<Qqp<_{\mathbb{Q}}qp<Q​q.

The first condition ensures that there are rational numbers on both sides of the cut. It excludes the two extreme cases in which the left-hand set is empty or contains every rational number.

Downward closure makes r^\hat{r}r^ an initial segment of Q\mathbb{Q}Q: once a rational number belongs to it, every smaller rational number must also belong to it. Thus the set describes a single boundary, rather than a collection with holes. In particular, every member of r^\hat{r}r^ is smaller than every member of Q∖r^\mathbb{Q}\setminus\hat{r}Q∖r^.

The final condition fixes how we treat a rational boundary. For a∈Qa\in\mathbb{Q}a∈Q, both {q∈Q∣q<Qa}and{q∈Q∣q<Qa or q=a} \{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q<_{\mathbb{Q}}a\} \quad\text{and}\quad \{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q<_{\mathbb{Q}}a\text{ or }q=a\} {q∈Q∣q<Q​a}and{q∈Q∣q<Q​a or q=a} are nonempty proper downward-closed subsets of Q\mathbb{Q}Q. Allowing both would give two descriptions of the same intended boundary. Requiring no greatest element excludes the second set and retains the first: the left-hand set always consists of rational numbers strictly below the boundary. The first set has no greatest element because, whenever p<Qap<_{\mathbb{Q}}ap<Q​a, the rational number p+Qa2\frac{p+_{\mathbb{Q}}a}{2}2p+Q​a​ lies strictly between ppp and aaa.

Definition 2 — Real numbers as Dedekind left sets

A real number is a Dedekind left set. The set of real numbers is RD={r^∈P(Q)∣r^ is a Dedekind left set}. \mathbb{R}_D=\{\hat{r}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Q})\mid\hat{r}\text{ is a Dedekind left set}\}. RD​={r^∈P(Q)∣r^ is a Dedekind left set}. For now, we denote real numbers by r^\hat{r}r^ to emphasise that they are sets of rational numbers. Each rational number aaa is represented by the real number a^={q∈Q∣q<Qa}. \hat{a}=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q<_{\mathbb{Q}}a\}. a^={q∈Q∣q<Q​a}.

Example 3 — The left set representing one half

The rational number 1/21/21/2 is represented by 12^={q∈Q∣q<Q(1/2)}. \widehat{\tfrac12}=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q<_{\mathbb{Q}}(1/2)\}. 21​​={q∈Q∣q<Q​(1/2)}. This set is nonempty because it contains 000, and proper because it does not contain 1/21/21/2. It is downward closed: if q<Qpq<_{\mathbb{Q}}pq<Q​p and p<Q1/2p<_{\mathbb{Q}}1/2p<Q​1/2, then q<Q1/2q<_{\mathbb{Q}}1/2q<Q​1/2. It has no greatest element, since for every member ppp, the rational number t=p+Q122 t=\frac{p+_{\mathbb{Q}}\tfrac12}{2} t=2p+Q​21​​ satisfies p<Qt<Q1/2p<_{\mathbb{Q}}t<_{\mathbb{Q}}1/2p<Q​t<Q​1/2. Thus it is a Dedekind left set.

By contrast, the set B={q∈Q∣q≤Q(1/2)} B=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid q\leq_{\mathbb{Q}}(1/2)\} B={q∈Q∣q≤Q​(1/2)} is nonempty, proper, and downward closed, but has greatest element 1/21/21/2. It is therefore not a Dedekind left set. Including the boundary is precisely what makes this example fail the final condition.

Order

A left set locates a number by recording the rationals below it. Moving the boundary to the right enlarges the set, so inclusion is the natural way to compare these real numbers.

Definition 5 — Equality and order of real numbers

Let r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​. Their equality is ordinary set equality, as in the definition of subsets and equality: r^=s^  ⟺  (∀q∈Q) (q∈r^  ⟺  q∈s^). \hat{r}=\hat{s}\iff(\forall q\in\mathbb{Q})\,(q\in\hat{r}\iff q\in\hat{s}). r^=s^⟺(∀q∈Q)(q∈r^⟺q∈s^). We define the non-strict order and strict order by r^≤s^  ⟺  r^⊆s^,r^<s^  ⟺  r^⊊s^.\begin{aligned} \hat{r}\leq\hat{s}&\iff\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{s},\\ \hat{r}<\hat{s}&\iff\hat{r}\subsetneq\hat{s}. \end{aligned}r^≤s^r^<s^​⟺r^⊆s^,⟺r^⊊s^.​ Thus r^<s^\hat{r}<\hat{s}r^<s^ means r^≤s^\hat{r}\leq\hat{s}r^≤s^ and r^≠s^\hat{r}\ne\hat{s}r^=s^. These orders on real numbers are distinct from the rational order <Q<_{\mathbb{Q}}<Q​ used inside each left set.

Proposition 6 — The real numbers are linearly ordered

For all r^,s^,t^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s},\hat{t}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^,t^∈RD​, the relation ≤\leq≤ satisfies the following properties.

  1. Reflexivity. r^≤r^\hat{r}\leq\hat{r}r^≤r^.
  2. Antisymmetry. If r^≤s^\hat{r}\leq\hat{s}r^≤s^ and s^≤r^\hat{s}\leq\hat{r}s^≤r^, then r^=s^\hat{r}=\hat{s}r^=s^.
  3. Transitivity. If r^≤s^\hat{r}\leq\hat{s}r^≤s^ and s^≤t^\hat{s}\leq\hat{t}s^≤t^, then r^≤t^\hat{r}\leq\hat{t}r^≤t^.
  4. Linearity. Either r^≤s^\hat{r}\leq\hat{s}r^≤s^ or s^≤r^\hat{s}\leq\hat{r}s^≤r^.
Proof.

The first three properties follow directly from the definitions of set inclusion and equality.

For linearity, suppose r^⊈s^\hat{r}\nsubseteq\hat{s}r^⊈s^, and choose p∈r^∖s^p\in\hat{r}\setminus\hat{s}p∈r^∖s^. For any q∈s^q\in\hat{s}q∈s^, we must have q<Qpq<_{\mathbb{Q}}pq<Q​p: equality would give p∈s^p\in\hat{s}p∈s^, and p<Qqp<_{\mathbb{Q}}qp<Q​q would also give p∈s^p\in\hat{s}p∈s^ by downward closure. Since p∈r^p\in\hat{r}p∈r^, downward closure of r^\hat{r}r^ now gives q∈r^q\in\hat{r}q∈r^. Thus s^⊆r^\hat{s}\subseteq\hat{r}s^⊆r^, proving linearity.

We use the earlier definitions of upper bounds and suprema, now with the order in Definition 5. In this construction, their conditions are simply statements about inclusion of sets.

Theorem 7 — Completeness of the Dedekind real numbers

Every nonempty subset A⊆RDA\subseteq\mathbb{R}_DA⊆RD​ that is bounded above has a supremum in RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​. Explicitly, sup⁡A=⋃r^∈Ar^. \sup A=\bigcup_{\hat{r}\in A}\hat{r}. supA=r^∈A⋃​r^.

Proof.

Let AAA be nonempty and let u^∈RD\hat{u}\in\mathbb{R}_Du^∈RD​ be an upper bound of AAA. Put s^=⋃r^∈Ar^={q∈Q∣(∃r^∈A) q∈r^}. \hat{s}=\bigcup_{\hat{r}\in A}\hat{r} =\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid(\exists\hat{r}\in A)\,q\in\hat{r}\}. s^=r^∈A⋃​r^={q∈Q∣(∃r^∈A)q∈r^}. We first check that s^\hat{s}s^ is a Dedekind left set.

Since AAA is nonempty, it contains some r^0\hat{r}_0r^0​, which is itself nonempty. Thus s^\hat{s}s^ is nonempty. Also, every r^∈A\hat{r}\in Ar^∈A is a subset of u^\hat{u}u^, so s^⊆u^≠Q\hat{s}\subseteq\hat{u}\ne\mathbb{Q}s^⊆u^=Q. Hence s^\hat{s}s^ is a proper subset of Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

If p∈s^p\in\hat{s}p∈s^ and q<Qpq<_{\mathbb{Q}}pq<Q​p, then p∈r^p\in\hat{r}p∈r^ for some r^∈A\hat{r}\in Ar^∈A. Downward closure of r^\hat{r}r^ gives q∈r^⊆s^q\in\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{s}q∈r^⊆s^. Thus s^\hat{s}s^ is downward closed.

Finally, if p∈s^p\in\hat{s}p∈s^, choose r^∈A\hat{r}\in Ar^∈A containing ppp. Since r^\hat{r}r^ has no greatest element, there is q∈r^q\in\hat{r}q∈r^ with p<Qqp<_{\mathbb{Q}}qp<Q​q. Then q∈s^q\in\hat{s}q∈s^ as well, so s^\hat{s}s^ has no greatest element. Therefore s^∈RD\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Ds^∈RD​.

For every r^∈A\hat{r}\in Ar^∈A, we have r^⊆s^\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{s}r^⊆s^, so s^\hat{s}s^ is an upper bound of AAA. If v^\hat{v}v^ is any other upper bound, then every r^∈A\hat{r}\in Ar^∈A is a subset of v^\hat{v}v^, and hence s^=⋃r^∈Ar^⊆v^. \hat{s}=\bigcup_{\hat{r}\in A}\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{v}. s^=r^∈A⋃​r^⊆v^. Thus s^≤v^\hat{s}\leq\hat{v}s^≤v^, proving that s^=sup⁡A\hat{s}=\sup As^=supA.

□

This reveals an advantage of Dedekind's definition: the least upper bound is obtained simply by taking a union. In our earlier treatment of real numbers, completeness was an axiom. Here we have chosen a different starting point, constructing real numbers as particular sets of rationals, so completeness follows as a theorem. Its status as an axiom or a theorem depends on the foundational system we use.

Corollary 8 — The real numbers are unbounded

The set RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​ is neither bounded above nor bounded below in itself. More precisely, for every r^∈RD\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^∈RD​ there are a^,b^∈RD\hat{a},\hat{b}\in\mathbb{R}_Da^,b^∈RD​ such that a^<r^<b^. \hat{a}<\hat{r}<\hat{b}. a^<r^<b^.

Proof.

Choose a∈r^a\in\hat{r}a∈r^ and c∈Q∖r^c\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\hat{r}c∈Q∖r^, and put b=c+Q1b=c+_{\mathbb{Q}}1b=c+Q​1. Downward closure gives a^⊆r^\hat{a}\subseteq\hat{r}a^⊆r^, and a∈r^∖a^a\in\hat{r}\setminus\hat{a}a∈r^∖a^ makes the inclusion strict. Every member of r^\hat{r}r^ is smaller than ccc, so r^⊆b^\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{b}r^⊆b^; this inclusion is strict because c∈b^∖r^c\in\hat{b}\setminus\hat{r}c∈b^∖r^. Hence a^<r^<b^\hat{a}<\hat{r}<\hat{b}a^<r^<b^.

Operations

We retain the Q\mathbb{Q}Q subscripts on rational addition, subtraction, and multiplication to distinguish them from the operations on hatted real numbers. Fractions and rational squares use their usual notation.

Definition 9 — Addition of real numbers

For r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​, define r^+s^={p+Qq∣p∈r^, q∈s^}. \hat{r}+\hat{s} =\{p+_{\mathbb{Q}}q\mid p\in\hat{r},\ q\in\hat{s}\}. r^+s^={p+Q​q∣p∈r^, q∈s^}.

The idea is to add rational numbers lying below the two boundaries. This again gives a Dedekind left set: sums exist because both sets are nonempty, and rational upper bounds of the summands give an upper bound for the sums. If t<Qp+Qqt<_{\mathbb{Q}}p+_{\mathbb{Q}}qt<Q​p+Q​q, then t−Qq<Qpt-_{\mathbb{Q}}q<_{\mathbb{Q}}pt−Q​q<Q​p, so t=(t−Qq)+Qqt=(t-_{\mathbb{Q}}q)+_{\mathbb{Q}}qt=(t−Q​q)+Q​q also belongs to the sum. Finally, increasing ppp within r^\hat{r}r^ increases the sum, so there is no greatest element.

Conversely, if t<Q1t<_{\mathbb{Q}}1t<Q​1, take p=q=t/2p=q=t/2p=q=t/2. Then p,q<Q1/2p,q<_{\mathbb{Q}}1/2p,q<Q​1/2 and p+Qq=tp+_{\mathbb{Q}}q=tp+Q​q=t. Remark 11 — Why multiplication needs a different definition

Replacing sums by arbitrary products does not work. For example, the set {p⋅Qq∣p∈1^, q∈1^} \{p\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}q\mid p\in\hat{1},\ q\in\hat{1}\} {p⋅Q​q∣p∈1^, q∈1^} is all of Q\mathbb{Q}Q, rather than 1^\hat{1}1^. Every t≥Q0t\geq_{\mathbb{Q}}0t≥Q​0 is obtained by taking p=−Q(t+Q1)p=-_{\mathbb{Q}}(t+_{\mathbb{Q}}1)p=−Q​(t+Q​1) and q=−Qtt+Q1q=\frac{-_{\mathbb{Q}}t}{t+_{\mathbb{Q}}1}q=t+Q​1−Q​t​, both of which are smaller than 111. If t<Q0t<_{\mathbb{Q}}0t<Q​0, take p=1/2p=1/2p=1/2 and q=2⋅Qtq=2\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}tq=2⋅Q​t.

In particular, two arbitrarily large negative members can produce arbitrarily large positive products. The proposed product is not a proper subset of Q\mathbb{Q}Q, so it is not a real number under our definition.

Definition 12 — Multiplication of real numbers

First, for any real number r^\hat{r}r^, define its negative by −r^={t∈Q∣(∃u∈Q∖r^) t<Q−Qu}. -\hat{r}=\{t\in\mathbb{Q}\mid(\exists u\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus\hat{r})\ t<_{\mathbb{Q}}-_{\mathbb{Q}}u\}. −r^={t∈Q∣(∃u∈Q∖r^) t<Q​−Q​u}. For nonnegative real numbers r^,s^≥0^\hat{r},\hat{s}\geq\hat{0}r^,s^≥0^, define r^⋅s^={t∈Q∣t<Q0 or (∃p∈r^)(∃q∈s^) (0<Qp∧0<Qq∧t<Qp⋅Qq)}. \hat{r}\cdot\hat{s} =\{t\in\mathbb{Q}\mid t<_{\mathbb{Q}}0\text{ or } (\exists p\in\hat{r})(\exists q\in\hat{s})\, (0<_{\mathbb{Q}}p\land0<_{\mathbb{Q}}q\land t<_{\mathbb{Q}}p\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}q)\}. r^⋅s^={t∈Q∣t<Q​0 or (∃p∈r^)(∃q∈s^)(0<Q​p∧0<Q​q∧t<Q​p⋅Q​q)}. For the remaining sign combinations, define r^⋅s^={−((−r^)⋅s^),r^<0^, s^≥0^,−(r^⋅(−s^)),r^≥0^, s^<0^,(−r^)⋅(−s^),r^<0^, s^<0^. \hat{r}\cdot\hat{s}=\begin{cases} -\bigl((-\hat{r})\cdot\hat{s}\bigr),&\hat{r}<\hat{0},\ \hat{s}\geq\hat{0},\\ -\bigl(\hat{r}\cdot(-\hat{s})\bigr),&\hat{r}\geq\hat{0},\ \hat{s}<\hat{0},\\ (-\hat{r})\cdot(-\hat{s}),&\hat{r}<\hat{0},\ \hat{s}<\hat{0}. \end{cases} r^⋅s^=⎩⎨⎧​−((−r^)⋅s^),−(r^⋅(−s^)),(−r^)⋅(−s^),​r^<0^, s^≥0^,r^≥0^, s^<0^,r^<0^, s^<0^.​

The idea is to multiply positive rational approximations first, where multiplication preserves order. We then include every rational below such a product, together with all negative rationals, to obtain a left set. If either factor is 0^\hat{0}0^, it has no positive members, so the product is exactly 0^\hat{0}0^. Positive rational upper bounds of the factors ensure that the product is proper; the strict inequality in its definition ensures that it has no greatest element.

Negation reflects the right-hand side of a cut to the left. Taking all rationals strictly below a reflected point removes a possible greatest element at a rational boundary. In particular, −a^=−Qa^-\hat{a}=\widehat{-_{\mathbb{Q}}a}−a^=−Q​a​ for rational aaa. The remaining cases of multiplication then implement the usual sign rules.

With the multiplication just defined, 2^⋅3^=6^. \hat{2}\cdot\hat{3}=\hat{6}. 2^⋅3^=6^.

Conversely, let t<Q6t<_{\mathbb{Q}}6t<Q​6. Negative ttt belongs to the product by definition. For t≥Q0t\geq_{\mathbb{Q}}0t≥Q​0, choose rational numbers t3<Qp<Q2,tp<Qq<Q3. \frac{t}{3}<_{\mathbb{Q}}p<_{\mathbb{Q}}2, \qquad \frac{t}{p}<_{\mathbb{Q}}q<_{\mathbb{Q}}3. 3t​<Q​p<Q​2,pt​<Q​q<Q​3. Such choices are possible by taking rational midpoints. Then p∈2^p\in\hat{2}p∈2^, q∈3^q\in\hat{3}q∈3^, both are positive, and t<Qp⋅Qqt<_{\mathbb{Q}}p\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}qt<Q​p⋅Q​q. Thus ttt belongs to the product, proving equality.

Example 14 — The square of the cut for the square root of two

Let r^\hat{r}r^ be the left set in Example 4. Then r^>0^\hat{r}>\hat{0}r^>0^ and r^⋅r^=2^. \hat{r}\cdot\hat{r}=\hat{2}. r^⋅r^=2^. Thus this construction does give a positive real number whose square is 2^\hat{2}2^, which we may denote by 2^\sqrt{\hat{2}}2^​.

Proof.

The set r^\hat{r}r^ contains all negative rationals and also 111, so r^>0^\hat{r}>\hat{0}r^>0^. If p,qp,qp,q are positive members of r^\hat{r}r^, put m=max⁡{p,q}m=\max\{p,q\}m=max{p,q}. Then p⋅Qq≤Qm2<Q2. p\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}q\leq_{\mathbb{Q}}m^2<_{\mathbb{Q}}2. p⋅Q​q≤Q​m2<Q​2. Consequently r^⋅r^⊆2^\hat{r}\cdot\hat{r}\subseteq\hat{2}r^⋅r^⊆2^.

Field

The operations on Dedekind left sets satisfy the field axioms from our earlier notes. Here these laws are properties of the construction, rather than additional assumptions about real numbers.

Proposition 15 — Field properties of the real numbers

The set RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​, with the addition and multiplication defined above, is a field. The elements 0^\hat{0}0^ and 1^\hat{1}1^ are distinct, and the following laws hold.

Addition.

  1. Closure. If r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​, then r^+s^∈RD\hat{r}+\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^+s^∈RD​.
  2. Associativity. For all r^,s^,t^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s},\hat{t}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^,t^∈RD​, (r^+s^)+t^=r^+(s^+t^). (\hat{r}+\hat{s})+\hat{t}=\hat{r}+(\hat{s}+\hat{t}). (r^+s^)+t^=r^+(s^+t^).
  3. Commutativity. For all r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​, r^+s^=s^+r^. \hat{r}+\hat{s}=\hat{s}+\hat{r}. r^+s^=s^+r^.
  4. Identity. For every r^∈RD\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^∈RD​, r^+0^=0^+r^=r^. \hat{r}+\hat{0}=\hat{0}+\hat{r}=\hat{r}. r^+0^=0^+r^=r^.
  5. Inverses. For every r^∈RD\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^∈RD​, its negative −r^-\hat{r}−r^ is a real number and r^+(−r^)=(−r^)+r^=0^. \hat{r}+(-\hat{r})=(-\hat{r})+\hat{r}=\hat{0}. r^+(−r^)=(−r^)+r^=0^.

Multiplication.

  1. Closure. If r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​, then r^⋅s^∈RD\hat{r}\cdot\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^⋅s^∈RD​. If neither factor is 0^\hat{0}0^, their product is not 0^\hat{0}0^.
  2. Associativity. For all r^,s^,t^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s},\hat{t}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^,t^∈RD​, (r^⋅s^)⋅t^=r^⋅(s^⋅t^). (\hat{r}\cdot\hat{s})\cdot\hat{t}=\hat{r}\cdot(\hat{s}\cdot\hat{t}). (r^⋅s^)⋅t^=r^⋅(s^⋅t^).
  3. Commutativity. For all r^,s^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^∈RD​, r^⋅s^=s^⋅r^. \hat{r}\cdot\hat{s}=\hat{s}\cdot\hat{r}. r^⋅s^=s^⋅r^.
  4. Identity. For every r^∈RD\hat{r}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^∈RD​, r^⋅1^=1^⋅r^=r^. \hat{r}\cdot\hat{1}=\hat{1}\cdot\hat{r}=\hat{r}. r^⋅1^=1^⋅r^=r^.

Distributivity. For all r^,s^,t^∈RD\hat{r},\hat{s},\hat{t}\in\mathbb{R}_Dr^,s^,t^∈RD​, r^⋅(s^+t^)=r^⋅s^+r^⋅t^. \hat{r}\cdot(\hat{s}+\hat{t}) =\hat{r}\cdot\hat{s}+\hat{r}\cdot\hat{t}. r^⋅(s^+t^)=r^⋅s^+r^⋅t^. By commutativity, this also gives the corresponding law for multiplication on the right.

Cantor's construction

Dedekind's construction describes a real number by the rationals below it. Cantor's construction instead uses rational sequences whose terms become arbitrarily close to one another. We again start with Q\mathbb{Q}Q, without assuming that the sequences already have real limits.

Cauchy sequences

Definition 16 — Rational sequences

A rational sequence is a function from the positive integers to Q\mathbb{Q}Q. We write it as (an)n≥1=(a1,a2,a3,…), (a_n)_{n\geq1}=(a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots), (an​)n≥1​=(a1​,a2​,a3​,…), or simply (an)(a_n)(an​), where an∈Qa_n\in\mathbb{Q}an​∈Q is its nnn th term.

Definition 17 — Cauchy sequences

A rational sequence (an)(a_n)(an​) is a Cauchy sequence if, for every ε∈Q\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}ε∈Q with ε>Q0\varepsilon>_{\mathbb{Q}}0ε>Q​0, there exists a positive integer NNN such that m,n≥N  ⟹  ∣am−Qan∣<Qε. m,n\geq N\implies\lvert a_m-_{\mathbb{Q}}a_n\rvert<_{\mathbb{Q}}\varepsilon. m,n≥N⟹∣am​−Q​an​∣<Q​ε.

Thus, however small a positive rational tolerance we choose, all sufficiently late terms are within that tolerance of one another. The definition compares terms with other terms, rather than with a presumed limit. Absolute values here are those of rational numbers.

Definition 18 — Equivalent Cauchy sequences

Two rational Cauchy sequences (an)(a_n)(an​) and (bn)(b_n)(bn​) are equivalent, written (an)∼(bn)(a_n)\sim(b_n)(an​)∼(bn​), if, for every ε∈Q\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}ε∈Q with ε>Q0\varepsilon>_{\mathbb{Q}}0ε>Q​0, there exists a positive integer NNN such that n≥N  ⟹  ∣an−Qbn∣<Qε. n\geq N\implies\lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n\rvert<_{\mathbb{Q}}\varepsilon. n≥N⟹∣an​−Q​bn​∣<Q​ε.

Equivalent sequences need not have the same terms, or even eventually agree. The idea is that their termwise difference becomes arbitrarily small, so they should represent the same real number.

Example 19 — Different sequences representing the same number

The sequences (an)=(0,0,0,…),(bn)=(1,12,13,…),bn=1n, (a_n)=(0,0,0,\ldots), \qquad (b_n)=\left(1,\frac12,\frac13,\ldots\right),\quad b_n=\frac1n, (an​)=(0,0,0,…),(bn​)=(1,21​,31​,…),bn​=n1​, are equivalent Cauchy sequences. The constant sequence is Cauchy because every difference is zero. Given a positive rational ε\varepsilonε, choose a positive integer N>Q2/εN>_{\mathbb{Q}}2/\varepsilonN>Q​2/ε. For m,n≥Nm,n\geq Nm,n≥N, ∣1m−Q1n∣≤Q1m+Q1n≤Q2N<Qε, \left|\frac1m-_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac1n\right| \leq_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac1m+_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac1n \leq_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac2N<_{\mathbb{Q}}\varepsilon, ​m1​−Q​n1​​≤Q​m1​+Q​n1​≤Q​N2​<Q​ε, so (bn)(b_n)(bn​) is Cauchy. Also, for n≥Nn\geq Nn≥N, ∣an−Qbn∣=1n≤Q1N<Qε. \lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n\rvert=\frac1n \leq_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac1N<_{\mathbb{Q}}\varepsilon. ∣an​−Q​bn​∣=n1​≤Q​N1​<Q​ε. Thus (an)∼(bn)(a_n)\sim(b_n)(an​)∼(bn​), although an≠bna_n\ne b_nan​=bn​ for every nnn.

Proposition 20 — Equivalence of Cauchy sequences is an equivalence relation

For rational Cauchy sequences (an)(a_n)(an​), (bn)(b_n)(bn​), and (cn)(c_n)(cn​), the relation ∼\sim∼ satisfies the following properties.

  1. Reflexivity. (an)∼(an)(a_n)\sim(a_n)(an​)∼(an​).
  2. Symmetry. If (an)∼(bn)(a_n)\sim(b_n)(an​)∼(bn​), then (bn)∼(an)(b_n)\sim(a_n)(bn​)∼(an​).
  3. Transitivity. If (an)∼(bn)(a_n)\sim(b_n)(an​)∼(bn​) and (bn)∼(cn)(b_n)\sim(c_n)(bn​)∼(cn​), then (an)∼(cn)(a_n)\sim(c_n)(an​)∼(cn​).

Thus ∼\sim∼ is an equivalence relation on the set of rational Cauchy sequences.

Proof.

Reflexivity follows from ∣an−Qan∣=0\lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}a_n\rvert=0∣an​−Q​an​∣=0, and symmetry from ∣bn−Qan∣=∣an−Qbn∣\lvert b_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}a_n\rvert=\lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n\rvert∣bn​−Q​an​∣=∣an​−Q​bn​∣.

For transitivity, suppose (an)∼(bn)(a_n)\sim(b_n)(an​)∼(bn​) and (bn)∼(cn)(b_n)\sim(c_n)(bn​)∼(cn​), and let ε>Q0\varepsilon>_{\mathbb{Q}}0ε>Q​0 be rational. Choose positive integers N1,N2N_1,N_2N1​,N2​ such that n≥N1  ⟹  ∣an−Qbn∣<Qε2,n≥N2  ⟹  ∣bn−Qcn∣<Qε2.\begin{aligned} n\geq N_1&\implies\lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n\rvert<_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac\varepsilon2,\\ n\geq N_2&\implies\lvert b_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}c_n\rvert<_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac\varepsilon2. \end{aligned}n≥N1​n≥N2​​⟹∣an​−Q​bn​∣<Q​2ε​,⟹∣bn​−Q​cn​∣<Q​2ε​.​ For n≥N=max⁡{N1,N2}n\geq N=\max\{N_1,N_2\}n≥N=max{N1​,N2​}, the triangle inequality for rational numbers gives ∣an−Qcn∣≤Q∣an−Qbn∣+Q∣bn−Qcn∣<Qε2+Qε2=ε.\begin{aligned} \lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}c_n\rvert &\leq_{\mathbb{Q}}\lvert a_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n\rvert+_{\mathbb{Q}}\lvert b_n-_{\mathbb{Q}}c_n\rvert\\ &<_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac\varepsilon2+_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon. \end{aligned}∣an​−Q​cn​∣​≤Q​∣an​−Q​bn​∣+Q​∣bn​−Q​cn​∣<Q​2ε​+Q​2ε​=ε.​ Hence (an)∼(cn)(a_n)\sim(c_n)(an​)∼(cn​).

Equivalence classes

Definition 21 — Equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences

Let C\mathcal{C}C be the set of rational Cauchy sequences. The equivalence class of (an)∈C(a_n)\in\mathcal{C}(an​)∈C is [an]={(bn)∈C∣(bn)∼(an)}. [a_n]=\{(b_n)\in\mathcal{C}\mid(b_n)\sim(a_n)\}. [an​]={(bn​)∈C∣(bn​)∼(an​)}. Any sequence belonging to [an][a_n][an​] is called a representative of this equivalence class.

An equivalence class simply collects all Cauchy sequences equivalent to a given one. By Proposition 20, choosing a different representative from the same class gives exactly the same collection: [an]=[bn]  ⟺  (an)∼(bn). [a_n]=[b_n]\iff(a_n)\sim(b_n). [an​]=[bn​]⟺(an​)∼(bn​). For example, the constant zero sequence and (1/n)(1/n)(1/n) belong to the same equivalence class. We need no further discussion of classes here: each [an][a_n][an​] is just a set of rational Cauchy sequences.

Definition 22 — Real numbers as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences

In Cantor's construction, a real number is an equivalence class of rational Cauchy sequences. We write RC={[an]∣(an)∈C}. \mathbb{R}_C=\{[a_n]\mid(a_n)\in\mathcal{C}\}. RC​={[an​]∣(an​)∈C}. A rational number qqq is represented by the class of the constant sequence (q,q,q,…)(q,q,q,\ldots)(q,q,q,…).

The subscript distinguishes this construction from the Dedekind real numbers RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​. An element of RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​ is a left set of rationals, whereas an element of RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​ is a set of equivalent Cauchy sequences.

Definition 23 — Order on the Cantor real numbers

For [an],[bn]∈RC[a_n],[b_n]\in\mathbb{R}_C[an​],[bn​]∈RC​, define [an]≤[bn]  ⟺  (∀ε∈Q, ε>Q0)(∃N≥1)(∀n≥N) an<Qbn+Qε. [a_n]\leq[b_n] \iff (\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q},\ \varepsilon>_{\mathbb{Q}}0) (\exists N\geq1)(\forall n\geq N)\, a_n<_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n+_{\mathbb{Q}}\varepsilon. [an​]≤[bn​]⟺(∀ε∈Q, ε>Q​0)(∃N≥1)(∀n≥N)an​<Q​bn​+Q​ε. Define the strict order by [an]<[bn]  ⟺  [an]≤[bn] and [an]≠[bn]. [a_n]<[b_n]\iff[a_n]\leq[b_n]\text{ and }[a_n]\ne[b_n]. [an​]<[bn​]⟺[an​]≤[bn​] and [an​]=[bn​].

Operations

Definition 26 — Addition and multiplication of Cauchy classes

For [an],[bn]∈RC[a_n],[b_n]\in\mathbb{R}_C[an​],[bn​]∈RC​, define addition and multiplication term by term: [an]+[bn]=[an+Qbn],[an]⋅[bn]=[an⋅Qbn].\begin{aligned} [a_n]+[b_n]&=[a_n+_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n],\\ [a_n]\cdot[b_n]&=[a_n\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n]. \end{aligned}[an​]+[bn​][an​]⋅[bn​]​=[an​+Q​bn​],=[an​⋅Q​bn​].​ Here the right-hand sides denote the equivalence classes of the sequences (an+Qbn)(a_n+_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n)(an​+Q​bn​) and (an⋅Qbn)(a_n\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}b_n)(an​⋅Q​bn​). For rational qqq, write [q][q][q] for the class of the constant sequence (q,q,q,…)(q,q,q,\ldots)(q,q,q,…); in particular, the zero and unit are [0][0][0] and [1][1][1].

The termwise sums and products are again Cauchy sequences, and replacing either sequence by an equivalent one gives an equivalent result. Thus these operations are well-defined on equivalence classes. We state the resulting properties without proof.

Proposition 27 — Field properties and completeness of the Cantor real numbers

The set RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​, with the addition and multiplication defined above, is a field. The elements [0][0][0] and [1][1][1] are distinct, and the following laws hold.

Addition.

  1. Closure. If x,y∈RCx,y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y∈RC​, then x+y∈RCx+y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx+y∈RC​.
  2. Associativity. For all x,y,z∈RCx,y,z\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y,z∈RC​, (x+y)+z=x+(y+z). (x+y)+z=x+(y+z). (x+y)+z=x+(y+z).
  3. Commutativity. For all x,y∈RCx,y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y∈RC​, x+y=y+x. x+y=y+x. x+y=y+x.
  4. Identity. For every x∈RCx\in\mathbb{R}_Cx∈RC​, x+[0]=[0]+x=x. x+[0]=[0]+x=x. x+[0]=[0]+x=x.
  5. Inverses. For every x∈RCx\in\mathbb{R}_Cx∈RC​, there is a real number −x-x−x such that x+(−x)=(−x)+x=[0]. x+(-x)=(-x)+x=[0]. x+(−x)=(−x)+x=[0].

Multiplication.

  1. Closure. If x,y∈RCx,y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y∈RC​, then x⋅y∈RCx\cdot y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx⋅y∈RC​. If neither factor is [0][0][0], their product is not [0][0][0].
  2. Associativity. For all x,y,z∈RCx,y,z\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y,z∈RC​, (x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z). (x\cdot y)\cdot z=x\cdot(y\cdot z). (x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z).
  3. Commutativity. For all x,y∈RCx,y\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y∈RC​, x⋅y=y⋅x. x\cdot y=y\cdot x. x⋅y=y⋅x.
  4. Identity. For every x∈RCx\in\mathbb{R}_Cx∈RC​, x⋅[1]=[1]⋅x=x. x\cdot[1]=[1]\cdot x=x. x⋅[1]=[1]⋅x=x.
  5. Inverses. For every x≠[0]x\ne[0]x=[0], there is a real number y≠[0]y\ne[0]y=[0] such that x⋅y=y⋅x=[1]. x\cdot y=y\cdot x=[1]. x⋅y=y⋅x=[1].

Distributivity. For all x,y,z∈RCx,y,z\in\mathbb{R}_Cx,y,z∈RC​, x⋅(y+z)=x⋅y+x⋅z. x\cdot(y+z) =x\cdot y+x\cdot z. x⋅(y+z)=x⋅y+x⋅z. By commutativity, this also gives the corresponding law for multiplication on the right.

Completeness. Every nonempty subset of RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​ that is bounded above has a supremum in RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​.

We use the earlier definitions of upper bounds and suprema, interpreted using the order on RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​. As in the Dedekind construction, completeness is a theorem about the constructed system. We omit the proofs here: establishing these properties, particularly completeness, would take us further into the foundations of analysis than we need for these set theory notes.

Other number systems

Isomorphism

Definition 28 — Isomorphisms of fields and ordered fields

Let FFF and GGG be fields. An isomorphism from FFF to GGG is a bijection ϕ:F→G\phi:F\to Gϕ:F→G preserving the field operations: for all x,y∈Fx,y\in Fx,y∈F, ϕ(x+Fy)=ϕ(x)+Gϕ(y),ϕ(x⋅Fy)=ϕ(x)⋅Gϕ(y),ϕ(0F)=0G,ϕ(1F)=1G.\begin{aligned} \phi(x+_F y)&=\phi(x)+_G\phi(y),\\ \phi(x\cdot_F y)&=\phi(x)\cdot_G\phi(y),\\ \phi(0_F)&=0_G,\\ \phi(1_F)&=1_G. \end{aligned}ϕ(x+F​y)ϕ(x⋅F​y)ϕ(0F​)ϕ(1F​)​=ϕ(x)+G​ϕ(y),=ϕ(x)⋅G​ϕ(y),=0G​,=1G​.​ If FFF and GGG are ordered fields, an ordered-field isomorphism also preserves order: x<Fy  ⟺  ϕ(x)<Gϕ(y). x<_F y\iff\phi(x)<_G\phi(y). x<F​y⟺ϕ(x)<G​ϕ(y). We say that the fields are isomorphic if such an isomorphism exists, and write F≅GF\cong GF≅G, specifying order preservation when relevant.

The subscripts identify the field in which an operation is performed. An isomorphism matches every element of one system with exactly one element of the other, while keeping arithmetic intact. The elements may look different, but corresponding calculations give corresponding answers.

Example 29 — Rational numbers on the complex plane

Let S={q+0i∣q∈Q}⊆C. S=\{q+0i\mid q\in\mathbb{Q}\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}. S={q+0i∣q∈Q}⊆C. These are the points on the real axis of the complex plane with rational real coordinate. With the usual complex addition and multiplication, SSS is a field. Define ϕ:Q→S,ϕ(q)=q+0i. \phi:\mathbb{Q}\to S,\qquad\phi(q)=q+0i. ϕ:Q→S,ϕ(q)=q+0i. This map is bijective and sends 000 to 0+0i0+0i0+0i and 111 to 1+0i1+0i1+0i. For rational p,qp,qp,q, ϕ(p+Qq)=ϕ(p)+ϕ(q),ϕ(p⋅Qq)=ϕ(p)ϕ(q).\begin{aligned} \phi(p+_{\mathbb{Q}}q)&=\phi(p)+\phi(q),\\ \phi(p\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}q)&=\phi(p)\phi(q). \end{aligned}ϕ(p+Q​q)ϕ(p⋅Q​q)​=ϕ(p)+ϕ(q),=ϕ(p)ϕ(q).​ Thus Q≅S\mathbb{Q}\cong SQ≅S. Intuitively, we have placed the rational number line inside the complex plane without changing its arithmetic. For example, (2+0i)(3+0i)=6+0i(2+0i)(3+0i)=6+0i(2+0i)(3+0i)=6+0i corresponds to 2⋅Q3=62\cdot_{\mathbb{Q}}3=62⋅Q​3=6. We may also order SSS by its real coordinates, making ϕ\phiϕ an ordered-field isomorphism.

The eleven field laws, the four order laws, and completeness give the sixteen properties used in our earlier description of the real numbers. A field satisfying the order laws is an ordered field; if every nonempty subset bounded above has a supremum in the field, it is a complete ordered field.

Theorem 30 — Uniqueness of the complete ordered field up to isomorphism

Any two complete ordered fields FFF and GGG are isomorphic as ordered fields. In fact, there is a unique ordered-field isomorphism ϕ:F→G\phi:F\to Gϕ:F→G.

Proof.

We will develop the proof in stages. The first step is to see that the correspondence on rational numbers is forced.

First step: matching rational numbers. In an ordered field FFF, the positive integer nnn is represented by nF=1F+F⋯+F1F⏟n terms. n_F=\underbrace{1_F+_F\cdots+_F1_F}_{n\text{ terms}}. nF​=n terms1F​+F​⋯+F​1F​​​. Set 0F0_F0F​ as usual and represent negative integers by additive inverses. The rational number q=m/nq=m/nq=m/n, with integers mmm and n>0n>0n>0, is represented by qF=mF⋅F(nF)−1, q_F=m_F\cdot_F(n_F)^{-1}, qF​=mF​⋅F​(nF​)−1, where (nF)−1(n_F)^{-1}(nF​)−1 denotes the multiplicative inverse of nFn_FnF​. Since 1F>F0F1_F>_F0_F1F​>F​0F​, we have nF>F0Fn_F>_F0_FnF​>F​0F​, so this inverse exists. Rational arithmetic shows that this representation is independent of the choice of m/nm/nm/n and gives a copy of Q\mathbb{Q}Q inside FFF. The same construction gives qGq_GqG​ in GGG.

Any field isomorphism ϕ:F→G\phi:F\to Gϕ:F→G must send 1F1_F1F​ to 1G1_G1G​. Preservation of addition then gives ϕ(nF)=nG\phi(n_F)=n_Gϕ(nF​)=nG​ for positive integers, and preservation of zero and additive inverses gives the same conclusion for every integer. Preservation of multiplication sends a multiplicative inverse to the inverse of the image, so ϕ(qF)=ϕ(mF⋅F(nF)−1)=mG⋅G(nG)−1=qG. \phi(q_F) =\phi\bigl(m_F\cdot_F(n_F)^{-1}\bigr) =m_G\cdot_G(n_G)^{-1}=q_G. ϕ(qF​)=ϕ(mF​⋅F​(nF​)−1)=mG​⋅G​(nG​)−1=qG​. Thus every possible isomorphism must agree with the canonical correspondence qF↦qGq_F\mapsto q_GqF​↦qG​ on the rational subfields. Extending this correspondence to all elements, using completeness, is the next stage of the theorem's proof.

Remark 31 — The two constructions give isomorphic real fields

The Dedekind and Cantor constructions both give complete ordered fields. Consequently, Theorem 30 gives RD≅RC \mathbb{R}_D\cong\mathbb{R}_C RD​≅RC​ as ordered fields. Under this isomorphism, the Dedekind left set q^\hat{q}q^​ corresponds to the class [q][q][q] of the constant rational sequence. The two constructions use different sets as their elements, but they have the same arithmetic and order structure.

Proposition 34 — Properties of the rational numbers

The rational numbers constructed above have the following properties.

  1. Ordered field. Q\mathbb{Q}Q satisfies all eleven field laws and all four order laws from our earlier notes. In particular, addition and multiplication are associative and commutative, multiplication distributes over addition, every rational has an additive inverse, and every nonzero rational has a multiplicative inverse.
  2. Integer embedding. The map a↦[a,1]a\mapsto[a,1]a↦[a,1] is injective and preserves addition, multiplication, zero, one, and order.
  3. Density. If x<Qyx<_{\mathbb{Q}}yx<Q​y, then x<Qx+Qy2<Qy. x<_{\mathbb{Q}}\frac{x+_{\mathbb{Q}}y}{2}<_{\mathbb{Q}}y. x<Q​2x+Q​y​<Q​y.
  4. Archimedean property. Every rational number is smaller than some positive integer, viewed as an element of Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

We state these properties without proof. Compared with the real numbers, the missing property is completeness. For example, A={q∈Q∣0≤Qq and q2<Q2} A=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}\mid0\leq_{\mathbb{Q}}q\text{ and }q^2<_{\mathbb{Q}}2\} A={q∈Q∣0≤Q​q and q2<Q​2} is nonempty and bounded above in Q\mathbb{Q}Q, but has no rational supremum. Its real supremum is 2\sqrt{2}2​, which is irrational. Thus rational numbers satisfy the first fifteen properties, but not the sixteenth.

Now assume that N\mathbb{N}N already exists with its usual arithmetic and order. Here we use the convention N={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}N={0,1,2,…} and mark its operations and order with the subscript N\mathbb{N}N.

On N×N\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}N×N, define an equivalence relation by (a,b)∼(c,d)  ⟺  a+Nd=c+Nb. (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+_{\mathbb{N}}d=c+_{\mathbb{N}}b. (a,b)∼(c,d)⟺a+N​d=c+N​b. An integer is an equivalence class [a,b][a,b][a,b] under this relation, and Z={[a,b]∣a,b∈N}. \mathbb{Z}=\{[a,b]\mid a,b\in\mathbb{N}\}. Z={[a,b]∣a,b∈N}.

The pair (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) represents the intended difference of aaa and bbb, without requiring subtraction in N\mathbb{N}N. For example, (3,1)(3,1)(3,1) and (4,2)(4,2)(4,2) represent the same integer. The notation [a,b][a,b][a,b] here refers to classes of natural-number pairs under this new relation, rather than the classes used to construct Q\mathbb{Q}Q. A natural number aaa is represented by [a,0][a,0][a,0].

For [a,b],[c,d]∈Z[a,b],[c,d]\in\mathbb{Z}[a,b],[c,d]∈Z, define [a,b]≤Z[c,d]  ⟺  a+Nd≤Nc+Nb,[a,b]<Z[c,d]  ⟺  a+Nd<Nc+Nb,[a,b]+Z[c,d]=[a+Nc, b+Nd],[a,b]⋅Z[c,d]=[a⋅Nc+Nb⋅Nd, a⋅Nd+Nb⋅Nc],−Z[a,b]=[b,a].\begin{aligned} [a,b]\leq_{\mathbb{Z}}[c,d] &\iff a+_{\mathbb{N}}d\leq_{\mathbb{N}}c+_{\mathbb{N}}b,\\ [a,b]<_{\mathbb{Z}}[c,d] &\iff a+_{\mathbb{N}}d<_{\mathbb{N}}c+_{\mathbb{N}}b,\\ [a,b]+_{\mathbb{Z}}[c,d] &=[a+_{\mathbb{N}}c,\ b+_{\mathbb{N}}d],\\ [a,b]\cdot_{\mathbb{Z}}[c,d] &=[a\cdot_{\mathbb{N}}c+_{\mathbb{N}}b\cdot_{\mathbb{N}}d,\ a\cdot_{\mathbb{N}}d+_{\mathbb{N}}b\cdot_{\mathbb{N}}c],\\ -_{\mathbb{Z}}[a,b]&=[b,a]. \end{aligned}[a,b]≤Z​[c,d][a,b]<Z​[c,d][a,b]+Z​[c,d][a,b]⋅Z​[c,d]−Z​[a,b]​⟺a+N​d≤N​c+N​b,⟺a+N​d<N​c+N​b,=[a+N​c, b+N​d],=[a⋅N​c+N​b⋅N​d, a⋅N​d+N​b⋅N​c],=[b,a].​ The zero and unit are 0Z=[0,0]0_{\mathbb{Z}}=[0,0]0Z​=[0,0] and 1Z=[1,0]1_{\mathbb{Z}}=[1,0]1Z​=[1,0].

Again, these definitions are independent of the representatives; we omit the checks. Swapping the entries gives the additive inverse. There is no multiplicative inverse operation on all nonzero integers.

Proposition 37 — Properties of the integers

The integers constructed above have the following properties.

  1. Commutative ring. Addition is associative and commutative, with zero and additive inverses. Multiplication is associative and commutative, with unit distinct from zero, and distributes over addition.
  2. Order and products. The order is linear and compatible with addition and multiplication by positive integers. There are no zero divisors: a product is zero only if at least one factor is zero.
  3. Natural-number embedding. The map a↦[a,0]a\mapsto[a,0]a↦[a,0] is injective and preserves addition, multiplication, zero, one, and order.
  4. Discrete order. For every integer zzz, there is no integer strictly between zzz and z+Z1Zz+_{\mathbb{Z}}1_{\mathbb{Z}}z+Z​1Z​.

These properties are stated without proof. Compared with Q\mathbb{Q}Q, the obstruction to being a field is the lack of multiplicative inverses: for example, 222 has no inverse in Z\mathbb{Z}Z. Passing to rational classes supplies these missing inverses.

Remark 38 — The familiar chain of number systems

The constructions give natural injective maps N↪Z↪Q↪R. \mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}. N↪Z↪Q↪R. They send a∈Na\in\mathbb{N}a∈N to [a,0][a,0][a,0], z∈Zz\in\mathbb{Z}z∈Z to [z,1][z,1][z,1], and q∈Qq\in\mathbb{Q}q∈Q to either its Dedekind left set q^\hat{q}q^​ or its constant-sequence class [q][q][q]. Here R\mathbb{R}R may mean either RD\mathbb{R}_DRD​ or RC\mathbb{R}_CRC​, which are isomorphic as ordered fields.

After identifying each number system with its image in the next, we write N⊆Z⊆Q⊆R. \mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. N⊆Z⊆Q⊆R. The literal constructions use different kinds of sets as their elements; these inclusions express the identifications provided by the embeddings.
